claim: Auxiliary α2δ subunits are important proteins for trafficking of voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV) at the active zones of synapses.
source: Auxiliary α2δ subunits are important proteins for trafficking of voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV) at the active zones of synapses.
evidence: This is a general statement about α2δ function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Post-translational proteolytic cleavage of α2δ is essential for their modulatory effects on the trafficking of N-type (CaV2.2) calcium channels.
source: We have previously shown that the post-translational proteolytic cleavage of α2δ is essential for their modulatory effects on the trafficking of N-type (CaV2.2) calcium channels (Kadurin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The probability of presynaptic vesicular release is reduced when an uncleaved α2δ is expressed in rat neurons.
source: We extend these results here by showing that the probability of presynaptic vesicular release is reduced when an uncleaved α2δ is expressed in rat neurons and that this inhibitory effect is reversed when cleavage of α2δ is restored.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The inhibitory effect of uncleaved α2δ on vesicular release is reversed when cleavage of α2δ is restored.
source: We extend these results here by showing that the probability of presynaptic vesicular release is reduced when an uncleaved α2δ is expressed in rat neurons and that this inhibitory effect is reversed when cleavage of α2δ is restored.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Asynchronous release is influenced by the maturation of α2δ−1.
source: We also show that asynchronous release is influenced by the maturation of α2δ−1, highlighting the role of CaV channels in this component of vesicular release.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CaV channels play a role in asynchronous vesicular release.
source: We also show that asynchronous release is influenced by the maturation of α2δ−1, highlighting the role of CaV channels in this component of vesicular release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing that α2δ−1 maturation affects asynchronous release.

claim: CaV2.2 co-immunoprecipitates preferentially with cleaved wild-type α2δ.
source: We present additional evidence that CaV2.2 co-immunoprecipitates preferentially with cleaved wild-type α2δ.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data.

claim: The proteolytic maturation increases the association of α2δ−1 with CaV channel complex.
source: Our data indicate that the proteolytic maturation increases the association of α2δ−1 with CaV channel complex and is essential for its function on synaptic release.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proteolytic maturation of α2δ−1 is essential for its function on synaptic release.
source: Our data indicate that the proteolytic maturation increases the association of α2δ−1 with CaV channel complex and is essential for its function on synaptic release.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 channels are particularly important for synaptic transmission in central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: Among the three families of CaV channels (CaV1, CaV2 and CaV3), the CaV2 family and more specifically CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 channels (generating P/Q and N-type currents, respectively) are particularly important for synaptic transmission in central and peripheral nervous systems (Dolphin, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 are targeted to presynaptic terminals where they are responsible for triggering vesicular release.
source: CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 are targeted to presynaptic terminals where they are responsible for triggering vesicular release (Catterall and Few, 2008; Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: CaV channels are formed of several subunits: the α1 subunit, that constitutes the Ca2+ selective pore and the voltage sensor, and auxiliary subunits β (cytoplasmic) and α2δ (extracellular).
source: CaVs are formed of several subunits: the α1 subunit, that constitutes the Ca2+ selective pore and the voltage sensor, and auxiliary subunits β (cytoplasmic) and α2δ (extracellular) (Flockerzi et al., 1986; Liu et al., 1996; Takahashi and Catterall, 1987; Witcher et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Four genes coding for α2δ subunits have been identified.
source: Four genes coding for α2δ subunits have been identified (Dolphin, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: α2δ subunits are translated into a single pre-protein α2δ and post-translationally cleaved into α2 and δ peptides, which remain attached by di-sulfide bonds.
source: They are translated into a single pre-protein α2δ and post-translationally cleaved into α2 and δ peptides, which remain attached by di-sulfide bonds (Dolphin, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: In α2δ−1 and −2, α2 contains a perfect metal ion adhesion site (MIDAS) motif essential for the interaction with α1 subunit.
source: In α2δ−1 and −2, α2 contains a perfect metal ion adhesion site (MIDAS) motif essential for the interaction with α1 subunit (Cantí et al., 2005; Hendrich et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The δ subunit is glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored to the plasma membrane.
source: and δ which is glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored to the plasma membrane (Davies et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The structure of the CaV1.1 channel complex has been recently determined using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: The structure of the CaV1.1 channel complex has been recently determined using cryo-electron microscopy and has identified binding domains between CaV1.1 and α2δ−1 including the interaction of the α2δ MIDAS motif with loop I of the first repeated domain of CaV1.1 (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy has identified binding domains between CaV1.1 and α2δ−1 including the interaction of the α2δ MIDAS motif with loop I of the first repeated domain of CaV1.1.
source: The structure of the CaV1.1 channel complex has been recently determined using cryo-electron microscopy and has identified binding domains between CaV1.1 and α2δ−1 including the interaction of the α2δ MIDAS motif with loop I of the first repeated domain of CaV1.1 (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis studies have confirmed a functional interaction between α2δ−1 and the first extracellular loop of CaV1.2.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis studies have confirmed a functional interaction between α2δ−1 and the first extracellular loop of CaV1.2 (Bourdin et al., 2017) and CaV2.2 channels (unpublished results).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis studies have confirmed a functional interaction between α2δ−1 and the first extracellular loop of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis studies have confirmed a functional interaction between α2δ−1 and the first extracellular loop of CaV1.2 (Bourdin et al., 2017) and CaV2.2 channels (unpublished results).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished results from the authors.

claim: α2δ subunits are important for the trafficking of α1 subunits and their function.
source: α2δ subunits are important for the trafficking of α1 subunits and their function, and they are also key proteins for synaptic function and synaptogenesis (Dickman et al., 2008; Eroglu et al., 2009; Hoppa et al., 2012; Saheki and Bargmann, 2009; Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: α2δ subunits are key proteins for synaptic function and synaptogenesis.
source: α2δ subunits are important for the trafficking of α1 subunits and their function, and they are also key proteins for synaptic function and synaptogenesis (Dickman et al., 2008; Eroglu et al., 2009; Hoppa et al., 2012; Saheki and Bargmann, 2009; Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The proteolytic maturation of α2δ−1 into disulfide-linked polypeptides α2 and δ is an essential post-translational step enabling its modulatory effect on the activation and trafficking of N-type calcium channels in neurons.
source: We have recently shown that the proteolytic maturation of α2δ−1 into disulfide-linked polypeptides α2 and δ is an essential post-translational step enabling its modulatory effect on the activation and trafficking of N-type calcium channels in neurons (Kadurin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Uncleaved α2δ−1 inhibits presynaptic calcium transient-triggered action potential (AP) in hippocampal neurons.
source: Indeed, we show that uncleaved α2δ−1 inhibits presynaptic calcium transient-triggered action potential (AP) in hippocampal neurons and that this effect is reversed by the cleavage of α2δ−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The inhibitory effect of uncleaved α2δ−1 on presynaptic calcium transient-triggered action potential is reversed by the cleavage of α2δ−1.
source: Indeed, we show that uncleaved α2δ−1 inhibits presynaptic calcium transient-triggered action potential (AP) in hippocampal neurons and that this effect is reversed by the cleavage of α2δ−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Overexpression of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 induced a decrease of 29 ± 6% in exocytosis compared to the control empty vector condition.
source: Overexpression of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 induced a decrease of 29 ± 6% in exocytosis compared to the control empty vector condition (n = 28 and 41, respectively; p=0.04) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1c with statistical analysis.

claim: Inducing controlled cleavage of α2(3C)δ−1 by co-expressing 3C-protease resulted in an increase of 53 ± 18% in exocytosis compared to α2(3C)δ−1 alone.
source: Conversely, inducing controlled cleavage of α2(3C)δ−1 by co-expressing 3C-protease resulted in an increase of 53 ± 18% in exocytosis compared to α2(3C)δ−1 alone (n = 41 and 16, respectively; p=0.014), thus completely reversing the inhibitory effect of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1b and 1c with statistical analysis.

claim: Co-expression of 3C-protease completely reverses the inhibitory effect of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 on exocytosis.
source: Conversely, inducing controlled cleavage of α2(3C)δ−1 by co-expressing 3C-protease resulted in an increase of 53 ± 18% in exocytosis compared to α2(3C)δ−1 alone (n = 41 and 16, respectively; p=0.014), thus completely reversing the inhibitory effect of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1b and 1c with statistical analysis.

claim: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis properties are determined by the number of vesicles available for rapid release (the readily-releasable pool - RRP) and the probability (Pv) that a vesicle in the RRP will undergo fusion in response to a single AP stimulus.
source: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis properties are determined by the number of vesicles available for rapid release (the readily-releasable pool - RRP) and the probability (Pv) that a vesicle in the RRP will undergo fusion in response to a single AP stimulus (Schneggenburger et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: RRP can be determined using a high frequency stimulation.
source: RRP can be determined using a high frequency stimulation (Ariel and Ryan, 2010; Ariel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: During a 20 AP stimulus at 100 Hz, the fluorescence of vGlut-pHluorin in presynaptic terminals rapidly increases and reaches a plateau phase corresponding to the RRP.
source: During a 20 AP stimulus at 100 Hz, the fluorescence of vGlut-pHluorin in presynaptic terminals rapidly increases and reaches a plateau phase corresponding to the RRP (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2a.

claim: No difference in RRP size was recorded between empty vector, α2(3C)δ−1 and α2(3C)δ−1 with 3C-protease conditions.
source: As summarized in Figure 2d, no difference was recorded between the three conditions (empty vector, α2(3C)δ−1 and α2(3C)δ−1 with 3C-protease: 6.9 ± 0.4, 6.2 ± 0.3 and 6.4 ± 0.5% of total pool, n = 22, 16 and 19, respectively, p=0.78), indicating that proteolytic maturation of α2δ−1 affects the Pv, rather than the size of the RRP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2d with statistical analysis.

claim: Proteolytic maturation of α2δ−1 affects the Pv, rather than the size of the RRP.
source: As summarized in Figure 2d, no difference was recorded between the three conditions (empty vector, α2(3C)δ−1 and α2(3C)δ−1 with 3C-protease: 6.9 ± 0.4, 6.2 ± 0.3 and 6.4 ± 0.5% of total pool, n = 22, 16 and 19, respectively, p=0.78), indicating that proteolytic maturation of α2δ−1 affects the Pv, rather than the size of the RRP.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect on RRP size.

claim: After the plateau phase corresponding to the RRP, an additional increase in fluorescence takes place during the stimulation, and continues for more than 500 ms after the end of the stimulus before reaching a stationary phase.
source: After the plateau phase corresponding to the RRP, an additional increase in fluorescence takes place during the stimulation, and continues for more than 500 ms after the end of the stimulus before reaching a stationary phase (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3a.

claim: The secondary increase in fluorescence after RRP results from a combination of RRP refilling and slow decay of the elevated intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: It was proposed that this secondary increase in fluorescence results from a combination of RRP refilling and slow decay of the elevated intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Ariel and Ryan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The late increase in fluorescence represents post-stimulus exocytosis.
source: This late increase in fluorescence occurs at lower rate than the initial increase and represents post-stimulus exocytosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Overexpression of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 induced a decrease of about 30% in delayed exocytosis compared to control empty vector condition.
source: Overexpression of uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 induced a decrease of about 30% in this phase of exocytosis compared to control empty vector condition (n = 22 and 31, respectively; p<0.001) (Figure 3b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3b-c with statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction of delayed exocytosis by uncleaved α2(3C)δ−1 is completely prevented by the co-expression of α2(3C)δ−1 with 3C-protease.
source: This reduction of delayed exocytosis is completely prevented by the co-expression of α2(3C)δ−1 with 3C-protease (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Transient expression of α2δ−1 in cell lines results in only a partial cleavage of wild type α2δ−1, such that a mixture of cleaved and uncleaved α2δ protein appears in the whole cell lysate.
source: We have previously shown that transient expression of α2δ−1 in cell lines results in only a partial cleavage of wild type α2δ−1, such that a mixture of cleaved and uncleaved α2δ protein appears in the whole cell lysate (WCL) (Kadurin et al., 2012, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The percentage of cleaved α2δ−1 in the co-immunoprecipitated fractions is ~4 fold higher than the percentage of cleaved α2δ−1 in the input WCL.
source: We performed co-immunoprecipitation of wild type α2δ−1 with CaV2.2 from tsA-201 cell WCL and found that the percentage of cleaved α2δ−1 in the co-immunoprecipitated fractions is ~4 fold higher than the percentage of cleaved α2δ−1 in the input WCL (from 10.0 ± 0.6% to 39.2 ± 1.6% in WCL and co-immunoprecipitated fractions, respectively, n = 3) (Figure 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Cleaved α2δ−1 has stronger association with the CaV pore-forming subunit than uncleaved α2δ−1.
source: We performed co-immunoprecipitation of wild type α2δ−1 with CaV2.2 from tsA-201 cell WCL and found that the percentage of cleaved α2δ−1 in the co-immunoprecipitated fractions is ~4 fold higher than the percentage of cleaved α2δ−1 in the input WCL (from 10.0 ± 0.6% to 39.2 ± 1.6% in WCL and co-immunoprecipitated fractions, respectively, n = 3) (Figure 4), suggesting stronger association of mature cleaved α2δ−1 with the CaV pore-forming subunit.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Over-expression of α2δ subunits increased Pv.
source: A previous study has shown that over-expression of α2δ subunits and knock-down of endogenous α2δ increased and decreased Pv, respectively (Hoppa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Knock-down of endogenous α2δ decreased Pv.
source: A previous study has shown that over-expression of α2δ subunits and knock-down of endogenous α2δ increased and decreased Pv, respectively (Hoppa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Uncleaved α2δ−1 (α2(3C)δ−1) reduces Pv.
source: In good agreement with this, our data show that uncleaved α2δ−1 (α2(3C)δ−1) reduces Pv, and co-expression of the 3C-protease restores the control Pv.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Co-expression of the 3C-protease restores the control Pv.
source: In good agreement with this, our data show that uncleaved α2δ−1 (α2(3C)δ−1) reduces Pv, and co-expression of the 3C-protease restores the control Pv.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pv is modulated by the number of CaV2 channels in each active zone.
source: Interestingly, Pv is modulated by the number of CaV2 channels in each active zone (Ermolyuk et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Uncleaved α2δ subunits reduced the amplitude of calcium transients triggered by a single AP stimulation, by interfering with the trafficking of CaV2 channels.
source: and we have previously shown that uncleaved α2δ subunits reduced the amplitude of calcium transients triggered by a single AP stimulation, by interfering with the trafficking of CaV2 channels (Kadurin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The active zone proteins Rab-3 interacting molecules (RIMs) and Munc-13 are critical in the orchestration of synaptic vesicular release.
source: The active zone proteins Rab-3 interacting molecules (RIMs) and Munc-13, critical in the orchestration of synaptic vesicular release, have been shown to control the targeting of CaV2 channels within presynaptic terminals (de Jong et al., 2018; Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: RIMs and Munc-13 control the targeting of CaV2 channels within presynaptic terminals.
source: The active zone proteins Rab-3 interacting molecules (RIMs) and Munc-13, critical in the orchestration of synaptic vesicular release, have been shown to control the targeting of CaV2 channels within presynaptic terminals (de Jong et al., 2018; Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: RIMs and Munc-13 control the size of the RRP.
source: These active zone proteins have also been shown to control the size of the RRP (Augustin et al., 1999; Calloway et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The RRP is defined as a small fraction of vesicles in a presynaptic terminal that is available for immediate release with a brief stimulus train.
source: The RRP is defined as a small fraction of vesicles in a presynaptic terminal that is available for immediate release with a brief stimulus train, and thus likely to equate to docked vesicles identified by electron microscopy (Ariel and Ryan, 2012; Rizzoli and Betz, 2005; Schneggenburger et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The RRP is likely to equate to docked vesicles identified by electron microscopy.
source: The RRP is defined as a small fraction of vesicles in a presynaptic terminal that is available for immediate release with a brief stimulus train, and thus likely to equate to docked vesicles identified by electron microscopy (Ariel and Ryan, 2012; Rizzoli and Betz, 2005; Schneggenburger et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and represents an inference from the definition.

claim: The size of the RRP measured in this study (6–7% of the total pool of vesicles) is in good agreement with previously described values of RRP in neonatal rodent hippocampal neuron synapses.
source: The size of the RRP we describe here, which is determined by the amplitude of the fluorescence of the plateau (6–7% of the total pool of vesicles) is in good agreement with previously described values of RRP in neonatal rodent hippocampal neuron synapses (Ariel and Ryan, 2010; Fernández-Alfonso and Ryan, 2006; Rizzoli and Betz, 2005).
evidence: This claim compares the current experimental data with previously published values.

claim: Wild-type α2δ subunits have no effect on the size of the RRP.
source: A previous study has shown that wild-type α2δ subunits have no effect on the size of the RRP (Hoppa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Uncleaved α2δ−1 does not affect the size of the RRP.
source: Consistent with that study, our data show that uncleaved α2δ−1 does not affect the size of the RRP indicating that, unlike RIMs and Munc13, α2δ−1 does not have the same dual function on synaptic vesicular release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Unlike RIMs and Munc13, α2δ−1 does not have the same dual function on synaptic vesicular release.
source: Consistent with that study, our data show that uncleaved α2δ−1 does not affect the size of the RRP indicating that, unlike RIMs and Munc13, α2δ−1 does not have the same dual function on synaptic vesicular release.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect on RRP size.

claim: α2(3C)δ−1 may reduce the trafficking of endogenous CaV2 channels into active zones.
source: It is likely that α2(3C)δ−1 reduces the trafficking of endogenous CaV2 channels into active zones, as we showed for exogenously expressed CaV2.2 (Kadurin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on previous findings.

claim: α2(3C)δ−1 can traffic alone into presynaptic terminals.
source: However, α2(3C)δ−1 can also traffic alone into presynaptic terminals (Kadurin et al., 2016), where it could then displace the endogenous α2δ interacting with channels in active zones, thus forming non-functional channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: α2(3C)δ−1 could displace the endogenous α2δ interacting with channels in active zones, thus forming non-functional channels.
source: However, α2(3C)δ−1 can also traffic alone into presynaptic terminals (Kadurin et al., 2016), where it could then displace the endogenous α2δ interacting with channels in active zones, thus forming non-functional channels.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: The finding that uncleaved α2δ interacts less than cleaved α2δ with CaV2.2 may indicate that α2(3C)δ−1 reduces the trafficking of endogenous CaV2 channels into active zones rather than displacing endogenous α2δ.
source: The finding here that uncleaved α2δ interacts less than cleaved α2δ with CaV2.2 may indicate that the former mechanism is more likely.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: α2δ subunits have a role in synaptogenesis, independently from their role as a CaV auxiliary subunit.
source: Several reports have also described a role for α2δ subunits in synaptogenesis, independently from their role as a CaV auxiliary subunit (Dickman et al., 2008; Eroglu et al., 2009; Kurshan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: α2δ subunits are extracellular proteins anchored to the plasma membrane via a GPI moiety.
source: α2δ subunits are extracellular proteins anchored to the plasma membrane via a GPI moiety (Davies et al., 2010) which makes them potentially good candidates to interact with extracellular ligands such as thrombospondins, low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein and α-neurexin (Eroglu et al., 2009; Kadurin et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: α2δ subunits are potentially good candidates to interact with extracellular ligands such as thrombospondins, low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein and α-neurexin.
source: α2δ subunits are extracellular proteins anchored to the plasma membrane via a GPI moiety (Davies et al., 2010) which makes them potentially good candidates to interact with extracellular ligands such as thrombospondins, low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein and α-neurexin (Eroglu et al., 2009; Kadurin et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and represents an inference from the structural properties.

claim: A direct interaction between α2δ and thrombospondin and its role in the mediation of synaptogenesis remains controversial.
source: Although a direct interaction between α2δ and thrombospondin and its role in the mediation of synaptogenesis remains controversial (Lana et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature showing conflicting results.

claim: α2δ subunits could play a role as an extracellular coordinator of synaptic function.
source: altogether these reports suggest that α2δ subunits could play a role as an extracellular coordinator of synaptic function.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from multiple cited studies.

claim: The modulation of presynaptic CaV channels by proteolytic cleavage of α2δ subunits could serve as an additional regulatory mechanism for their complex synaptic functions at the post-translational level.
source: Furthermore, the modulation of presynaptic CaV channels by proteolytic cleavage of α2δ subunits could serve as an additional regulatory mechanism for their complex synaptic functions at the post-translational level.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings of the study.

claim: CaV2 channels and BK potassium channels are part of multi-molecular complexes in neurons.
source: CaV2 channels and BK potassium channels are known to be part of multi-molecular complexes in neurons (Berkefeld et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: α2δ−1 interacts with BK channels.
source: α2δ−1 has very recently been shown to interact with BK channels, and this interaction was found to reduce the stability of CaV2.2 channels at the plasma membrane by preventing α2δ−1 interacting with CaV2.2 channels (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The interaction between α2δ−1 and BK channels reduces the stability of CaV2.2 channels at the plasma membrane by preventing α2δ−1 interacting with CaV2.2 channels.
source: α2δ−1 has very recently been shown to interact with BK channels, and this interaction was found to reduce the stability of CaV2.2 channels at the plasma membrane by preventing α2δ−1 interacting with CaV2.2 channels (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: BK channels control neurotransmitter release by shortening the AP duration and reducing Ca2+ influx into presynaptic elements at neuro-muscular junctions.
source: Functionally, BK channels were shown to control neurotransmitter release by shortening the AP duration and reducing Ca2+ influx into presynaptic elements at neuro-muscular junctions (Protti and Uchitel, 1997; Yazejian et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The presence of BK channels in presynaptic boutons has been disputed.
source: Although their presence in presynaptic boutons has been disputed (Hoppa et al., 2014), BK channels are also expressed in axons from central neurons (Debanne et al., 2011; Johnston et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature showing conflicting results.

claim: BK channels are expressed in axons from central neurons.
source: Although their presence in presynaptic boutons has been disputed (Hoppa et al., 2014), BK channels are also expressed in axons from central neurons (Debanne et al., 2011; Johnston et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: α2δ−1 interacts with NMDA glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
source: Furthermore, α2δ−1 has also recently been shown to interact with NMDA glutamate receptors (NMDARs) (Chen et al., 2018), albeit via a C-terminal domain of α2δ−1 that is beyond the GPI-anchor attachment site and would therefore not be present in a mature GPI-anchored form (Davies et al., 2010; Kadurin et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The interaction between α2δ−1 and NMDARs occurs via a C-terminal domain of α2δ−1 that is beyond the GPI-anchor attachment site and would therefore not be present in a mature GPI-anchored form.
source: Furthermore, α2δ−1 has also recently been shown to interact with NMDA glutamate receptors (NMDARs) (Chen et al., 2018), albeit via a C-terminal domain of α2δ−1 that is beyond the GPI-anchor attachment site and would therefore not be present in a mature GPI-anchored form (Davies et al., 2010; Kadurin et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and represents an inference from structural knowledge.

claim: The interaction between α2δ−1 and NMDARs promotes the trafficking of the NMDARs to synaptic sites between peripheral dorsal root ganglion neurons and dorsal horn neurons in the spinal cord.
source: This interaction was found to promote the trafficking of the NMDARs to synaptic sites between peripheral dorsal root ganglion neurons and dorsal horn neurons in the spinal cord and is involved in the development of neuropathic pain (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The interaction between α2δ−1 and NMDARs is involved in the development of neuropathic pain.
source: This interaction was found to promote the trafficking of the NMDARs to synaptic sites between peripheral dorsal root ganglion neurons and dorsal horn neurons in the spinal cord and is involved in the development of neuropathic pain (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Synchronous stimulated release is often followed by a delayed release occurring after the end of the stimulus, also called asynchronous release.
source: Synchronous stimulated release is often followed by a delayed release occurring after the end of the stimulus, also called asynchronous release (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Kaeser and Regehr, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Asynchronous release is thought to be activated by residual Ca2+ remaining in the presynaptic terminal after the stimulation.

claim: The source of Ca2+ responsible for the initiation of synchronous release is voltage-gated calcium channels within the active zone.
source: Although the source of Ca2+ responsible for the initiation of synchronous release is indisputably identified from many studies as voltage-gated calcium channels within the active zone (Catterall and Few, 2008; Dolphin, 2012; Nakamura et al., 2015; Zamponi et al., 2015), the source of Ca2+ involved in asynchronous release remains uncertain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Asynchronous release is reduced in hippocampal presynaptic terminals when uncleaved α2δ−1 (α2(3C)δ−1) is expressed.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The inhibitory effect of uncleaved α2δ−1 on asynchronous release is abolished when 3C-protease is co-expressed.
source: We show that asynchronous release is reduced in hippocampal presynaptic terminals when uncleaved α2δ−1 (α2(3C)δ−1) is expressed, and this inhibitory effect is abolished when 3C-protease is co-expressed.

claim: Asynchronous release is mediated by Ca2+ influx generated by CaV localized at the presynaptic terminals.
source: Together with our previous report showing that the proteolytic cleavage of α2δ is critical for the functional trafficking of CaV2.2 channels to the presynaptic terminals (Kadurin et al., 2016), our data demonstrate that asynchronous release is mediated by Ca2+ influx generated by CaV localized at the presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the current experimental data combined with previous findings.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.
